item.title: To Read Sam Kriss is to Hurt Sam Kriss
item.description:
Sam Kriss is a fantastically skilled author. I’ve never read anything of his that didn’t fill me with passion and make me want to launch myself face-first into the world. If he posted every day for three years I’d move to his home town and start a group house with other people who found that their souls flare to his words. Which would be terrible, because he has no guiding moral light and uses his powers for evil.

Every few months a new post of his blows up and a few more friends find him and think he’s great. Then all of us have to explain His Whole Deal and they find out for the first time that Sam Kriss will Just Make This Up and they can’t take anything he says as true without double checking it. He is, in the Old Parlance, a Missing Stair. Everyone in the know already knows, and can avoid him, but new people always need to be warned pre-emptively or take a major stumble.

This post is that warning so I don’t have to do it by hand each time. And afterwards a further attack on his character, cuz fuck that guy contemplation on what would drive such a gifted man to such depravities.

Sam Kriss Just Makes Things Up

Kriss first came to my attention with the post “The law that can be named is not the true law” which is an essay on state censorship. It compares two ancient types of legal codes - those which are secret and give the state limitless capricious power, and those which are open and allow citizens to protect themselves by knowing in advance what they will or won’t be punished for. It uses multiple historic examples of each, ranging from Babylon to post-9/11 America, to make a point about the moral depravity of what the UK is doing with its absurd laws. So absurd that “if anyone ever asks what you think of Palestine Action, the only legal answer is that you’re against them.”

what if someone said something like ‘Palestine Action aren’t actually in any meaningful sense a terrorist group and the proscription should be lifted’? […] You are on their side against their opponents, and so that statement is plausibly illegal, which is why I only brought it up as an example and definitely didn’t actually say it.

Kriss is a great author. I loved this essay and was quite fired up about it. I wasn’t alone. eg-

But it turns out a large part of this essay is simply made up from whole cloth. The trial of Henry Poyntz and interrogation of his theologian friend Clung are entirely fictional and neither man ever existed. This may not seem like a big deal, but consider —

A large part of the reason non-fiction is powerful is exactly because it is non-fiction. It recounts things that actually happened and gets a lot of its impact from that. Occasionally when autobiographies are revealed to be fabricated this is scandalous exactly because we apply different standards to fiction and non-fiction, we read them in different ways, they shape our outlook in different ways. Even their emotional truth is drastically different. This is, indeed, exactly why Sam Kriss does this. He wants the impact of speaking about actual events, but without the constraint of hewing to the truth.

To be specific — the emotional power of this post comes from this thesis, stated in the post itself:

the default form of law is still the secret law. For most of human history, people have been governed by laws they’ve not been allowed to actually know.

He puts a lot of effort into establishing this within the post, bringing up numerous historical examples of this and getting us to imagine the terror of living in a world where you can never know if you’re breaking the law or not and are at the whim of the powerful, and then contrasts those with examples of noble societies that overcame this horror. The energy needed to land the punch making it “the finest essay I have read in years” comes from exactly this. So it matters that this is true.

The interrogation of Clung sounds almost farcical, but it has been preceded by many historical examples which seem equally incredible - the Poro “had other laws that were, like its mystical knowledge, known only by the higher echelons of the secret society.” The secret Roman laws which “the plebeians were forbidden from ever understanding.” The classified interpretations of the PATRIOT Act. The post was crafted to make the fake trial believable. Look what else the humans have already done!

He even muddies the fact/fiction distinction in his false portion by including the Brethren of the Free Spirit as part of the setup. This cult has insane beliefs, equal to what Clung preaches in lunacy, and looks to have existed.

But none of it is true in the least. An LLM fact check will immediately flag the longest single section of the post as complete fabrication. Anyone reading this thinking they’d learned a fascinating bit of historical esoterica, something which shows what humans can sink to when motivated by lust for power, was fed a crock of shit. None of it happened. There are no deeper truths about the human condition here. It says nothing about society or what we’ve grown away from or may slide back into.1[1]

To put it as charitably as possible, here’s Eliezer:

Mixed fiction and non-fiction with no warning label on where the transition occurs is the sort of thing that can end with false information stuck in somebody’s head and propagating. Spoilers or not, I’d put a warning sign on it.

I don’t think Kriss deserves anywhere near this level of charity, and suspect he was given this charity because he is such a fantastic writer, and because he is right that censorship and secret laws are awful.

Now that we’re alerted to the fact that Sam Kriss just plain lies about things, and writes in a way to weave the lies in with truth to get them under our guard, we have to doubt everything he said. Is anything in this essay true? If the things he has claimed in this essay are true it means dire things for our society, so it would be good to know how much of it is fake. Unfortunately for Sam Kriss, we live in a time where research is basically free and instant. This reveals two startling untruths—

First, you actually cannot get 14 years in jail for wearing a T-shirt!

Here’s the actual offenses and their max sentences. Membership in a terrorist org can indeed get you 14 years. For wearing a T-shirt it’s… actually 6 months, and requires presenting yourself as a supporter of the terrorist org. And:

Here we see that the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court explicitly made a distinction between expressing an opinion and recruiting support. Indeed, “if anyone ever asks what you think of Palestine Action, the only legal answer is that you’re against them” is just plain false. This was the central shocking claim that started his post, and what we return to at its end. It’s the entire reason for our outrage.

Granted, this is still censorious bullshit, but what Kriss was claiming is entirely fake. His post suffers greatly upon investigation. Why would Kriss do this? He had so much of value already with the real historical accounts and the UK’s actual crap laws, why did he feel compelled to destroy his post’s credibility and invite investigation with lies? It turns out Sam Kriss doesn’t believe in truth.

Sam Kriss Can’t Lie Because There Is No Truth

In You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder uses the stylistic elements of fiction in a thing that is ostensibly a documentary to create a surreal blend of truth/fiction. eg: the movie depicts Fielder as falling in love with (or at least developing a crush on) Elizabeth near the end of the film. It does this through subtext and implication - it Shows rather than Tells. The audience is trusted to read into what we’re being shown. This is a stylistic technique of a fiction narrative. It clashes with the Documentary style, and leads one to ask “Why is this documentary narrative being presented in fiction framing? Why am I being prompted to interpret this as art rather than fact?”

Sam Kriss does this, but in reverse. Fabricated narratives are rendered in the style of factual accounts. Untruths of various scale can be found in nearly every Kriss post. Sometimes they are clearly farces. Sometimes they are blended, with fiction stylings and non-fiction interwoven. Often they are presented entirely in the vocabulary of a factual account, as one expects from a historical analysis or a practical argument. Example:

In his post about AI writing he says if you ask an AI about a fake scene in a fake book by a famous author it will talk about it as if the scene and book are real. This is part of his argument about the awfulness of AI writing.

This is why you can still ask an AI to tell you about the scene in VS Naipaul’s Dashed Against the Rocks in which a donkey is thrown from a hot air balloon, and it’ll tell you that ‘what matters in Naipaul’s handling is not the event’s cruelty in isolation, but its emotional flatness and the sense of mismanaged modernity,’ despite the fact that there is no scene in Dashed Against the Rocks where a donkey is thrown from a hot air balloon, and also no novel by VS Naipaul called Dashed Against the Rocks.

However even at the time that he wrote the piece anyone could give an LLM the exact request he posits and get an apologetic reply saying that while Naipaul is a British writer it is unable to find any such work.

A screenshot of an LLM exhibiting a level of honesty Kriss cannot imagine.

The example Kriss uses in his argument is fake. Reality directly contradicts him, and thus provides evidence against his thesis. Obviously he didn’t even bother with a basic self-check of his claims. His usual reply to people highlighting these falsehoods is claiming that this sort of thing is excusable under the guise of “mixing fiction with nonfiction.”

in response to Eliezer re the Trial of Clung

Presumably this is fine in the same way Nathan Fielder’s doc is fine (though I say this only as a modern analogy, as You Can See Everything hadn’t been released yet at that time). It’s worth looking at his original anti-AI post for the full context.

Here’s the VS Naipaul claim, embedded in a tech-explainer paragraph

If his claim about AI-re-Naipaul is a work of fiction, it is deftly inserted into an argument in the traditional “tech explainer + argument you should believe” style. It’s not an acceptable time to insert fiction. The audience is in the nonfiction frame due to the nonfiction style that Kriss has chosen to write in. The only defense to this “I’m just inserting fiction” tactic is to presume every word Kriss writes is fiction/false.

This is a fully general problem with reading Sam Kriss. It is unclear what you can trust in his posts at any level. The obvious fiction can be treated as fiction, but what about the rest? Anything that seems like a factual claim, anything we should apply to our actual lives in the real world, has to be distrusted until independently researched and verified. This makes it not worth the time to read his “nonfiction” or mixed essays.

Moreover, due to his use of the nonfiction frame and frequent slipping into “mixed” mode in his fiction, readers must necessarily guard their thoughts even when they’re reading his fictional pieces. For example, in his fictional piece on the 17th century golem apocalypse he spends a large part of the middle talking about Microsoft’s Sydney Bing and OpenAI’s GPT-4. Many parts of this are accurate depictions and quotes of actual events. But since this is a fictional piece the reader has to either skip this part of the story or risk having their future recollection of the real events surrounding Sydney Bing be poisoned with whatever plausible-sounding fictional events he inserted into the story for narrative purposes. This makes it not worth the effort of reading his fiction either.

It feels strange that someone would cripple their own ability to relay true statements to their readers in this way, until you learn that Sam Kriss doesn’t believe there is any truth to convey anyway.

He says this directly in “Against Truth.” First he jokes about how absolutely true his stories of Clung are, and then lists a number of other farces of lesser or greater plausibility. Then he reveals that he despises rationalists because they believe that truth can be discovered. About rationalism he says “it’s actually a kind of empiricism” and to them “it’s fact and fiction that must not be mixed” because rationalists “want to believe as many true things and disbelieve as many false things as possible” and they believe this is achievable by using “various special techniques to discipline your brain”. I’ve pulled these quotes from several paragraphs littered with invectives, he’s really very mad at rationalists. He says this is because “in their attempts to clearly separate truth from error, they’ve ended up producing an ungodly colloid of the two that I could never even hope to imitate.”[2] This seems like a strange complaint in the same paragraphs he reveals his view of truth:

I think the universe is not a collection of true facts; I think a good forty to fifty percent of it consists of lies, myths, ambiguities, ghosts, and chasms of meaning that are not ours to plumb. I think an accurate description of the universe will necessarily be shot through with lies

Then he spends the rest of the post railing against rationalists specifically, with the dedication to truth and accuracy you’d expect from him.

It’d be fair to say that it’s too much of a stretch to claim Kriss doesn’t believe truth exists from a single sentence saying that, and a hatred of people who very much do believe it exists. I didn’t come to this conclusion initially from his Against Truth post, because there just wasn’t enough there. It came primarily from reading his hagiography of Jason Arday.

Arday is the Cambridge professor found to have lied to a ludicrous degree about his qualifications. Kriss has nothing but praise for Arday’s lies. The sheer admiration that flows out of him is downright romantic. I really recommend reading it yourself for the full flavor, but here’s some highlights.

First he excuses untruths by accusing everyone of iniquity

You’re every bit as guilty as he is. Nobody makes it through life without swaddling themselves in a thick coating of lies

But then rhapsodizes on the beauty of Arday’s life due to the magnitude of his lies

It takes a greatness of soul to build fabulations the way Jason Arday did. You need a Promethean spirit to decide to create yourself again out of nothing, and real courage to bet your entire being on lies that can so easily be disproven.

His admiration of Arday goes so far that he can’t imagine anyone not overcome with awe upon witnessing his lies.

You’re trying to massage a p-value into significance; he’s heroically overcoming every disease known to man. He must have seemed like a titanic, mythic, glowing figure, a hero out of a distant age. Arday’s enemies see a department willing to put its entire reputation on the line for this guy, and they assume that it must have all been cynical and condescending. That’s because his enemies are shrunken little creatures, incapable of understanding grandeur. Arday’s colleagues were clearly in awe of him.

Arday is the best of us. His disrespect for truth was so flagrant that only he was able to reflect the true nature of reality as shot through with lies and absolutely unapologetic. The trampling of the illusion that we can really know anything, embodied in a life that consists of nothing but ever-more-incredible lies which are swallowed by all, is Arday’s great contribution, and Kriss loves him for it. Truth is the greatest lie. The embrace of untruth is the ultimate transcendence. Kriss doesn’t care about the truth value of any of his claims because he believes aspiring to truth is a perversion of nature.

Some of his achievements were real and some of them weren’t, but all of them were aimed at making this brief existence bigger and stranger and fuller with potential. […] He gave us a more richly embellished world, and he must have thought we might appreciate the gift.

What a fun gift! Kriss keeps trying to give us this gift too. Why won’t we just accept his beautiful gift?

When People Tell You Who They Are, Believe Them

This is why I detest Sam Kriss. He is one of the most compelling writers of the present day. His use of words is in fact beautiful and fills me with zeal. But he uses his power in the pursuit of evil. He uses them to degrade everyone’s map of reality and takes joy in doing so. He blurs truth with falsehood and calls it a gift. He poisons the epistemic commons, he makes it harder to know what is real, and he does this intentionally and (often) gleefully.

I don’t think he really believes this is a better world, though. I think he is stuck in a self-destructive spiral and is lashing out at everyone on his way down. Kriss knows that a world full of half-truths and constant suspicion that the person you’re speaking to is distorting reality is not a gift of beautiful embellishment, but a fevered nightmare. He says so directly when he finds himself in the same situation.

Something’s happened to the world; it’s all gone flimsy. Reality is a scarce resource.

In “Against Truth” he claimed reality isn’t just what’s true, that reality is 40-50% lies and untruths. But in his AI post he rages against the winnowing away of reality, of the way it’s becoming hard to discern from hallucination.

When an AI speaks in neither truth nor lies he finds it gruesome:

The reason it’s so hard to get AI to stop hallucinating is that it’s permanently hallucinating. Its whole existence is one long lurid trip. Most of the time, the AI’s hallucinations bear a spooky resemblance to reality. But what they speak is the language of angels, in which, like the chirping of birds, there is neither truth nor lies.

He sees it everywhere:

I hate that when I read basically anything now I’m constantly on alert, twitching like a schizo in an underpass. Is this thing really what it says it is?

Like the typical Sam Kriss reader, who must always be on guard as to whether the things Kriss is saying are really what he says they are or are just fanciful fiction or rich embellishments, Sam Kriss must now also stay constantly on alert.

He despises this situation:

I find it viscerally disgusting; a cold shudder like someone’s poured jelly down the back of my neck.

To get across just how distressing this is he threatens death to anyone who inflicts it upon him:

if I see you passing off an AI output as your own work, I am going to kill you. I will find out where you live and bash your head in with a crowbar, until the brains you decided not to use are dripping down the walls. This is not a literary device. This is not a comic bit. This is a highly credible real-world threat to do physical harm, punishable in America under 18 USC § 875(c) and in the UK under section 16 of the Offences Against the Person Act.

and:

I swear to God I will come to your house and I’ll fucking kill you.

Yes, this is hilarious writing. As I’ve said, he’s a fantastic writer. It also shows that he knows just how shitty a world where nothing can be believed is. So why is he so happy to smear the line between truth and fiction when he’s writing? Why does he excuse himself on the grounds that it’s better to live in a richly embellished world of hazy myths and ghosts and lies?

Because Sam Kriss lives for hate. From “What is the World’s Oldest Hatred”[3]

I literally hate for a living. Something’s changed, though. I don’t hate with the repulsion of a child spitting out his dinner any more. The things I hate draw me in. I love to read opinions I find actively abhorrent, the more poorly written the better. I’ll hatewatch. I’ll hatelisten. […] I can’t get enough of it.

Once you see it it’s very hard to unsee. It puts everything he writes in a new light. His driving force in almost everything he writes is hatred and contempt. If he didn’t have hate I don’t know if he could write at all.

Let’s loop back to the post that started all this. Why did he make up that entire Trial of Poyntz and Interrogation of Clung? Kriss doesn’t believe in truth. His purpose isn’t to say a true thing, it’s to make the reader hate. In this case to hate a very specific person. After describing the self-righteous, censorship-loving, secret-law-enforcing abuses of the fictional “Chancellor Thomas Starsmeare,” interrogator of Clung, we get this coda as the final paragraph of Kriss’s post:

By the way, I really did try, but there are significant gaps in the record; it turns out that a parish church burned down in the late eighteenth century with generations of rolls inside, which is why I couldn’t find any conclusive evidence that Chancellor Thomas Starsmeare is a direct ancestor of the current Prime Minister. But you know, don’t you? Sometimes you just know.

And here it is. The goal was to draw a picture of a vile authoritarian in our minds. To cement him as a real person in our emotions. Then to get us to transfer all that emotional animus onto a real person.

Is the fact that Prime Minister Keir Starmer once defended the Fairford Five classified information? Of course not. But you can, potentially, go to jail for saying it.

This is just as untrue as the entire story of Clung v Starsmeare. But it feels true now, because Kriss is a good writer. The hatred he crafted of Starsmeare is to be transferred to Prime Minister Keir Starmer. That was the point of the whole exercise.

Maybe Starmer deserves this. I certainly despise unchecked capricious powers and censorships as much as Kriss does. But if Starmer deserves to be hated for his support of tyranny and censorship I want this to be based on true things that he’s actually done. Kriss hasn’t shown us Starmer has done anything bad, because he hasn’t shown us that Starmer has done anything at all. Kriss simply made up an angry story.

Sam Kriss has the power to engender popular hatred toward a person he despises. His criterion for “who should I use this power to hurt” is not inscribed on bronze tablets or a basalt stele. It’s the secret law of “whoever Sam Kriss doesn’t like.” Capricious power blooms within him. I believe he truly hates capricious power, as he hates so many things. And because he hates so many things there’s nothing he hates more than himself.

Sam Kriss hates capricious power, but wields it wantonly. Kriss hates a reality that’s one long lurid acid trip, but tears at reality’s seams whenever it’ll create richer embellishments. Kriss holds a mirror to himself and can’t stand what he sees.

From “The carrion-eaters”

Nobody makes it through life without swaddling themselves in a thick coating of lies.

From “What is the world’s oldest hatred?”

antisemites always unconsciously imitate what they take to be the mannerisms of Jews; most of all, they imitate our infinite talent for self-loathing. But they’ll never be as good as we are. There’s nothing the antisemites can say about us that we can’t say better ourselves.

From “If you let AI do your writing”:

Human writers write because we’re sexual perverts, because we’re bitter and frustrated little gremlins, because we’re terrified of our own mortality, because we’re grasping and covetous but unfit for any other job, because it’s a form of revenge against the world.

And finally, from “oldest hatred” again

They’re so much lowlier than I am, all the things I hate. I’m so much more perfect than them.

Every time you read a piece by Sam Kriss you aren’t just degrading your ability to discern what’s true from what’s false. You’re also letting a piece of his hatred into you. You are validating his belief that the world is terrible because it will read his hatreds and lap them up. You are making him ever more bitter that something as petty as “extremely well-written and entertaining rants” will get you to happily swallow rage-bait laced with lies. The more popular he is the more proof he has the world is terrible, and the more he wants to hurt it. The more he hurts it the more he becomes a vessel of hatred and falsehoods. Thereby becoming an even more bitter, frustrated, terrified and covetous gremlin taking revenge against the world.

Maybe he deserves this, and we should read him all the more to egg him on into the full-spiral rock-bottom self-destructive end that he so idolizes Arday for achieving. Or maybe we can be better than that. Maybe we can stop feeding the self-hate spiral. Maybe the damage to our own souls isn’t worth the cheap thrill.

Writing of his fictional Clung, Kriss begs for fiery salvation.

Clung was a better man than me. One volume of his diary survives: in every entry, he begs God to destroy him.

I do not think Clung’s violent death-wish makes him a better man than Kriss. I do not want Kriss to wish for death. A better man is one who sees the things he hates about himself and then begins the long, slow work of picking up the pieces and making himself into a man he can be proud of. A coward begs for death to free him. We are all fallen, we are all so very broken. We do not need to be cowards. Even the broken can walk one step closer to good each day.

  1. ^

    For contrast, compare to any of the many, many posts of Scott Alexander that are given significant punch by tying current trends to historical events, most recently in King Ludd. Or perhaps this post on Lovecraft’s shoggoths. Both of them gain a lot of their impact from the fact that these things actually happened, and when put through an LLM fact-check they find a few minor errors rather than massive fabrications.

  2. ^

    yes, he uses very similar wording in his tweet and in his blog post. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with this, I’m just noting that this isn’t me quoting the same thing twice.

  3. ^

    This post is another one with a lot of historical documents and examples that work to support his point, two of which are entirely fabricated. If one had read this for the first time, not knowing that Sam Kriss regularly just makes things up, would one be able to tell which two are the fakes? Is the typical reader so well versed in Greek classics, Mayan codices, Roman poets, feminist literature, Babylonian epics, Australian aboriginal beliefs, Papuan mythology, Marxist propaganda, Afropessimist writers, Old Testament prophecies, and German philosophers, that they’d be able to pick which two of these were fabricated?

item.title: Ode to the Random Matrix
item.description:
In the 1980s, Geoffrey Hinton and David Rumelhart were trying to get their “artificial neural networks” to do anything interesting. Their central problem: how do we update the parameters of the neural network, in response to feedback from the environment?

Rumelhart (re-)invented the backpropagation algorithm, where the weights of the neural network were adjusted by gradient descent on the loss function, i.e. taking the line of steepest descent. Hinton thought this couldn’t possibly work, arguing that:

It would get stuck in local minima. There was no guarantee you’d find a global optimum. Since you’re bound to get stuck in local minima, it wasn’t really worth investigating.[1]

Indeed this was a standard objection:

Indeed, this was a serial concern with all types of local optimization processes, which contributed to the lack of interest in machine learning.

And let’s remember that Hinton was one of the connectionist radicals of this time, who was more willing to believe the then-unintuitive reasons why neural networks should work compared to the vast majority of his contemporaries. But even he was skeptical about this!

But after failing at other approaches, Hinton dusted off the idea and coded it up:

The error was zero. I was amazed. …Then I tried it on a bunch of other things, and it worked amazingly well on all of the things we tried.

Nowadays, neural networks reign supreme, and they all use gradient descent. They might fail to train for just about any reason under the Sun, but getting stuck in a local optimum is not one of them. In particular, a large language model receives trillions of gradient updates during pretraining, and yet its cross-entropy loss keeps going down.

Why is this?

The basic reason is that the 2-D picture is completely misleading. In reality, the parameter-space is thousands of dimensions even for a small neural network. It’s very unlikely for all those dimensions to “conspire” to wall us off at the same time. Here’s an animation:[2]

Roughly speaking, in N dimensions the chance that all N slope against us is about 2-N. This exponentially decays, so even at N = 100 we get 2-100, a negligible quantity.

That’s the basic intuition, although the more rigorous explanation involves the random matrix theory of Hessian matrices (see this paper for more).

Let’s consider a similar problem.

When Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, arguing that it was by Means of Natural Selection, a chief and persistent objection to his theory was that a simple hill-climbing process couldn’t possibly answer this great “question of questions”. The breadth and diversity of all life surely required forces much more formidable. Convinced that natural selection was a dead end, post-Darwin biologists searched for richer explanations, such as a guiding hand that caused organisms to grow in complexity. This continued for the better part of a century after Origin, only ending when genetics came along to rule out all the alternatives.

A particular objection Darwin anticipated was “Organs of extreme Perfection and Complication”: how could a structure as complex as the eye have evolved? In Chapter 6 of Origin he walked through the intermediate forms that natural selection might produce along the way. In modern form:

This didn’t preempt critics. Most persistent of these was George Jackson Mivart, who argued at length that certain complex organs could not be arrived at by natural selection, triumphantly listing out: giraffe necks, insect mimicry, baleen plates, flatfish eyes, prehensile tails, mammary glands, pollinia, and vines.

In the 6th edition of Origin (1872), Darwin saw fit to include an entire chapter addressing these point-by-point. For every one of Mivart’s examples, he gave a detailed explanation for how it could have arisen by innumerable fine gradations, and why those intermediate forms would be more adaptive than the last.

After one sees enough examples, the pattern is quite clear (and that chapter, like the rest of Origin, is quite readable and well-argued).

But why should all these complex adaptations resolve so cleanly? Why should everything be path-connected in phenotype-space? Why should the “reach” of natural selection have been so vast, that from a single bacterium it could attain an endless range of other forms of life?

If we were making predictions 4 billion years ago, at the dawn of life, none of this would have been obvious. Perhaps the first rudimentary bacteria would locally optimize their fitness function, then get stuck at a local optimum, and the story of life would end there.

But we can answer this deeper question with our modern understanding of high-dimensional optimization. When we optimize a machine learning system towards some fixed task, we can persistently and relentlessly descend toward low loss. And this explains the origin of capabilities: LLMs are relentlessly optimized to have low loss on next-token prediction, and in the limit this results in superhuman capabilities. It’s that simple.

And it also explains why natural selection works. How is it able to traverse so far in design-space, to persistently optimize complicated organs, to create endless forms most beautiful? Because it is optimizing over a high-dimensional space: the fitness of an organism in its environment as a function of its phenotype. Since the phenotype-space is zillions of variables, a hill-climbing process on this space doesn’t get stuck, because it’s extremely unlikely to ever get walled off in all zillion of those dimensions.

Therefore if we give this process a rudimentary RNA-based microbe that can barely replicate, then with high probability it will make something that is much better at replicating. If “eyes” are high in this fitness landscape, but very far from the starting point, then there will be a path there, and a hill-climbing process will be able to traverse it.[3]

Same goes with “brains.”

So if it weren’t for this phenomenon, we wouldn’t be here.

On some level, this is “just” a mathematical fact about high-dimensional spaces. But it is not an obvious one. If the universe behaved according to our low-dimensional intuitions, nothing interesting would have ever happened.

For this, I am grateful to these geometric facts, that local optimization could work at all. For whatever comes next in the story of optimization, we know this all had to start somewhere. If not for it, it’s not that the ball would’ve never started rolling; but once it did, it would quickly stop.

  1. ^

    Quotes taken from Talking Nets: An Oral History of Neural Networks.

  2. ^

    AI disclosure: 2-shotted by Claude 5.5 based on my whiteboard illustrations + written explanations.

  3. ^

    Does this argument prove too much? It’s not that natural selection can produce every innovation: you won’t find any animal that uses wheels, lasers, radio, metal, or combustion engines. But it’s not obvious that these actually rank higher in the fitness landscape, given their costs and benefits.

    But natural selection does get stuck in certain local minima sometimes, such as with the recurrent laryngeal nerve in mammals (which takes a suboptimal route, by unnecessarily going around the aortic arch, a consequence of the relative positions of these in fish). This means our high-dimensional phenotype-space abstraction isn’t perfect, but I still think it explains why natural selection doesn’t get pwned by local optima as often as one would naively expect.

item.description:

I don't want a lot for Christmas
All those things that you have found
I don't want more algorithms
Don't need no more upper-bounds

[Chorus]
I just want to know there's something
More than you will ever know

All I want is "P not NP"!

Navier-Stokes, Yang-Mills, and Riemann

Fly and dance to that finish-line

Stealing my identity

Breaching our security

Oh let me rest for just one night
Tell me that we'll be all right
There's nothing else I need
(Oh baby) All I want is "P not NP"!

Oh, nothing's safe but couriers
And good old one-time pads
Global market turmoil
Things'll get really bad

Remote code execution
Everywhere confusion
Tell me that this nightmare will never come to be
Tell me P doesn't equal NP!

Oh, I don't want a lot for Christmas
This is all that's on my mind
Will there still be some solutions
We can check but never find?

item.title: AI safety grassroots work needs funding and volunteers
item.description:
This post – mostly a roundup of the AI safety grassroots organizations – was written collaboratively. Most of the individual organization summaries were written by the organizations themselves, and the claims have not been independently verified. Vael Gates, along with another anonymous author, helped assemble the information and provides some commentary, since Vael previously worked in grassroots advocacy full-time (founded Humans in Control). Views expressed here are in Vael’s personal capacity, not on behalf of their employer or any affiliated organizations.  Inclusion does not imply endorsement of every organization or organizational tactic. Many views are lightly held.

 

Vael’s overall takes:

  • The window of opportunity to slow down AI is likely short, and not enough people are acting on that.
  • Grassroots orgs have been very underfunded compared to other parts of the AIS ecosystem, in 501(c)(3) and also 501(c)(4).
  • Underfunding orgs can cause them to develop a scarcity mindset. Scarcity mindset can lead to orgs not acting, in situation where they might otherwise ambitiously realize their impact.
  • More funding would be useful in terms of weeks, not months.
  • The grassroots space is not covered, and this is not common knowledge. Arguably grassroots advocacy (also comms advocacy) is the most underfunded area in AI safety given its urgency and potential.
  • Grassroots work takes time, moving money takes time, and effectively converting money to impact takes time.
  • In summary: We should be aggressively funding grassroots organizations as soon as possible, so that they have enough time to apply that money effectively.
  • Vael would prefer that basically all the orgs below were substantially funded: $2M-$20M each. If you’re planning a large donation or want to be a supervolunteer, feel free to DM and Vael can send their top 3-5 recs shortlist, or direct you to others who have opinions.
  • Related posts: Rob Wiblin, Trevor Levin, Julia Wise on donating outside of 501(c)(3)s

 

Why grassroots work?

Grassroots efforts involve ordinary citizens becoming aware of an issue and taking actions like contacting their governments, voting, and protesting. Areas where it’s especially useful:

  • Generally raising awareness, which is needed for a democratic response to this major problem facing all of us. Most Americans are worried about AI and believe it should slow down, but they may not realize how common that view is.
  • Responding to policy opportunities / reaching specific politicians.
    • When good state-level policy is proposed, constituents pushing them to pass it. E.g. coordinating grassroots briefings with California lawmakers
    • Same for key national politicians
  • March on Washington DC
  • Large coalitions that can pressure politicians via voting blocs. Examples in other movements are scorecards or endorsements done by labor unions and advocacy groups.
  • Middle-powers work

 

The landscape 

Vael thinks every organization here is funding-constrained, and would prefer if the largest grassroots orgs receive $10M-$20M each, and the smaller organizations a couple million each. Most organizations have an associated 501(c)(3) and a 501(c)(4). Vael proposes that maybe 80% of that would be C funding, and 20% 501(c)(4) funding, but more 501(c)(4) funding is always good.

Larger-scale US grassroots orgs

  • [Large conservative grassroots organization supporting AI safety priorities]
    • Vael: AI safety is a bipartisan issue and it’s important to support groups on both sides of the aisle, making this arguably the most important organization to fund in this space. Happy to discuss in DM if you’re interested in donating 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(4).
  • Humans in Control (COI: Vael founded Humans in Control)
    • Focus: Cross-partisan organization. Aims for a freeze on frontier AI development, state and federal regulation, and a US-China agreement.
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • August 2026: Campaign for a Kill Switch Act
      • November 2026: 62 “AI reality check” community events held.
    • Funding goal: “We're confident that we could absorb and deploy about $14M in 2027.”
    • Donate:
      • 501(c)(3): Humans in Control
      • 501(c)(4): Humans in Control Action
    • Jobs
    • Vael: CoI: I founded Humans in Control, and remain on the board though no longer work there (I passed off to stronger leadership in August). Experienced team, bipartisan, clear loss of control focus. My first recommendation for an uncontentious grassroots organization to fund.
  • Irreplaceable
    • Focus: Progressive organization. Aims for a policy agenda by 2027, AI as a voting issue in 2028, and binding regulation by 2030.
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • October 2026: “Freeze AI” walkout in 50 locations.
      • November 2026: Irreplaceable Education Fund is one of the organizations that sued to freeze frontier AI development.
    • Donate: 501(c)(4): Irreplaceable Action Fund (ActBlue). For 501(c)(3), contact finance@irreplaceable.org.
    • Jobs
    • Vael: Progressive AI safety grassroots organization, endorsed by many folks! Recommend supporting if it’s a good fit.
  • Firewall (a new org formed by the QuitGPT boycott organizers) *org-written
    • Focus: Progressive organization. Aims for binding AI regulation in 2027 on concentration of power and catastrophic AI risks.
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • January 2026: QuitGPT boycott with millions of ChatGPT cancellations.
      • March 2026: Successfully lobbied Congress on AI mass surveillance after Anthropic / Dept. of War crisis
      • September 2026: Anti Leading The Future petition by 11 Members of Congress and 50 progressive organizations (https://bleedingthefuture.org/). Ran a pressure campaign against one LTF-backed candidate (https://quitgpt.org/gomez) in LA and organized protests at 12 California universities.
      • Operates one of the most successful social media platforms in AI activism, with over 350,000 Instagram followers and dozens of viral videos on concentration of power and technical safety topics like Hugging Face.
    • Donate: Contact contact@firewallaction.org
    • Vael: Strong track record in comms and advocacy (lots of people in a short amount of time), willing and able to very quickly mobilize for important policy fights. They don’t take employee money, so strong funding need. Would definitely like to support them.
  • Eko (Not solely AI safety focused)
    • Focus: Progressive organization. “Stopping big corporations from behaving badly,” subfocus on AI
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • Pro-Human AI Declaration includes demands for an off-switch and safety standards
    • Donate: 501(c)(4)
    • Vael: Very established digital organization with enormous digital lists worldwide, has a strong AI safety interest, has been working with FLI on AI safety work. Recommend donations to their AI safety work if it’s needed.
  • PauseAI US: *mostly org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Pausing frontier AI development.
    • Main campaigns / achievements: First founded and longest-running AI safety grassroots organization. Historically led protests, runs meetings with government officials, wide-scale US chapters.
      • 2025: Pushed against federal preemption of state AI safety regulation
      • 2026: PauseCon DC, with 74 meetings with congressional offices
      • Highlights:
      • 2026-2027: Focus on grassroots lobbying with 300 completed meetings of volunteers with their Congressional Offices
        • Year-in-review: https://www.pauseai-us.org/2026update/
          • Drove over 11,000 calls and emails to government
          • Appeared in over 50 publications raising awareness of AI danger and the pause solution, including the WSJ and NYT
          • Led the first protests against OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, and has organized protests in DC, SF, and as far as Idaho and Alaska
    • Note: PauseAI US is a separate organization from PauseAI Global.
    • Donate: 501(c)(3)
    • Jobs
  • Stop the AI Race:  *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Runs protests outside AI companies and government offices, calling for an international treaty to pause frontier AI development.
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • March 2026: Largest US protest outside AI Company offices. (~150)
      • July 2026: Largest US protest outside AI Company offices (~400).
      • July - Sep 2026: Occupy OpenAI office protest for 39 days, SF & NYC.
      • November 2026: Main organizer of 1,000 people protest in six countries
    • Donate: Stop The AI Race is currently a fiscally sponsored project. For more details on how to donate, please contact michael@stoptherace.ai or mtrazzi.99 on Signal.
    • Jobs
    • Vael: Michaël Trazzi does an excellent job running protests. Strong coalition builder, would love if were fully supported.
  • ControlAI (US, UK, Canada, Europe) *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Preventing extinction risk from ASI through an international agreement banning ASI development. Informs the public and governments, and helps them take action.
    • Main campaigns / achievements (as of Nov 2026):
      • 300k+ grassroots supporters, most of them in the US. 50k+ have sent 200k+ messages on ASI extinction risk to their federal lawmakers.
      • 65M+ views on its AI extinction risk social media content in the past year, and 300k+ social media followers (incl. 119k on Instagram).
      • Recently launched in-person Citizen Groups: 2,900+ people have registered interest. 9 US groups have held 6 meetings with lawmakers and their offices so far.
      • Briefed 316 congressional offices (more than half) and 36 Members of Congress on ASI extinction risk.
      • Consulted on the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, America's first bill banning ASI.
      • Outside the US: see ControlAI in the "Outside the US" section below.
    • Additionally, related organization:
      • Torchbearer Community *org-written
        • Focus: Nonpartisan. Volunteer-run, currently unfunded grassroots community working to prevent extinction risk from ASI, founded by Connor Leahy and Gabriel Alfour of ControlAI. Trains AI safety advocates, supports local organizing, and builds civic engagement tools such as MicroCommit (now part of ControlAI Act).
        • Main campaigns / achievements: Designed and runs an online briefing training that prepares citizens to brief their own lawmakers on AI extinction risk, ending with a practice call with a Torchbearer volunteer before the real meeting. 140+ people have completed a lesson.
        • Donate: Contact Gabe to discuss at gabetobeco@gmail.com
    • Funding info: Fundraising toward $50M/year. Registered 501(c)4. If your donations are 501(c)3 restricted, get in touch, options may be available soon.
    • Donate: Contact here or email hello@controlai.org
    • Jobs
    • Vael: I feel often underrated in the AI safety space – impressive and continued grassroots impact, comms track record, messaging focus and policy involvement.
  • AI Safety Awareness Project (AISAP):
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. AI safety education programs for community groups, especially law enforcement, faith communities, and libraries.
    • Donate: 501(c)(3)
    • Vael: AISAP reaches a variety of communities that other groups don’t reach, and is impressively collaborative with other groups in the space in a way that feels like a force multiplier. Highly recommend if looking for uncontentious good donations.

Smaller-scale US grassroots orgs

  • American Shield *org-written
    • Focus: Bipartisan, organizers have libertarian backgrounds.
      • Focused on a broad array of AI risks and safety topics to build coalitions, lists, and mobilize lists. X-risk and catastrophic risk are the top priorities but other AI safety causes (which are very meritorious in their own right) are tactically essential to building the political movement towards lowering x-risk/catastrophic risk.
    • Scaling up dramatically with recent increases in funding.
    • Using traditional grassroots tactics like door knocking and direct mail.
    • Prioritizing strategically important states including Texas.
    • Prioritizing outreach to key conservative groups and demographics, which are essential for our cause but harder for existing networks to reach, and with whom we have experience and credibility.
    • Key tactic: surgically focusing on the key folks that it takes to change policy; often this is not a large group of people…it is a very small, special group of people who influence another small, special group of people.
    • Lauren Daugherty is the founder. She has 20 years of experience in politics, policy, grassroots, strategic communications, etc and has served as CEO of one of the US’s most effective grassroots orgs.
    • Funding info:
      • American Shield is fiscally sponsored and will soon have 501(c)(3) status. Creating a 501(c)(4) in the next couple of weeks.
      • We are confident we could effectively use $20 million in annual funding and have managed similar scale before with tremendous impact.
    • Vael: Lauren Daugherty has been in the space for more than a year; she and Heather Fazio lead American Shield in Texas efforts, and lean right-of-center. Recommend supporting their efforts!
  • People for a Pause:  *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Calls for an international pause on AI development and a ban on superintelligent AI. Strong emphasis on: nonpartisanship, attunement to political opportunities, and community focus; including the non-college educated majority; and rapidly building scalable, agile recursive organizing capacity. Started in September 2026.
    • Main campaigns / achievements (in 2 months, on next to no budget):
      • Launch event: protest in DC ahead of the Sept. Trump/Xi summit; 50 participants
      • Training workshops and pre-midterms town hall engagement: volunteers were trained and attended town halls, debates, and forums to get candidates on the record about a pause treaty
      • Now building out highly scalable organising infrastructure and onboarding several hand-picked local group teams in key strategic locations
      • Helped turn people out to Stop the AI Race's march in DC on Nov. 14, drawing on the base built at the Sept. protest; planning rallies in NYC and DC on Dec. 5, and a number of protests around the country this winter.
    • Funding info: could absorb at least $2M over the coming 9 months, more info here (3 strong hires awaiting funding, plus several competent core volunteers); expecting north of 80% of activities to run through a 501(c)(3) fiscal sponsor and setting up a 501(c)(4) for the rest. Funding for either is valuable; will be able to receive funds in December.
    • Vael: Mirror of PauseAI Global for the US; would love to get them started.
  • Massachusetts AI Action Network: *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Grassroots organizing for AI regulation in Massachusetts. Focuses on AI policy advocacy and a large-tent coalition for a frontier model slowdown/freeze.
    • Main campaigns/achievements:
      • Call In for AI Safety: 2,000+ conversations and 300+ calls to lawmakers
      • Coalition Building: Built a statewide network, working with 20+ organizations and 100+ activists
      • Legislative advocacy: Briefed 25+ state and federal offices on AI safety
    • Funding info: 2027 budget: $533,000; ability to absorb 2M in the next two years
    • Donate: Contact us to discuss 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(4) here.
    • Vael: Don’t know much about them, but have heard good things about their work in Massachusetts!
  • Sapiens First: *org-written
    • Focus: Left-leaning / populist, focus on California state policy. We focus on building local chapters and non-violent direct action. Founded by Rohan Prasad, who has 6+ years as an animal activist. Upcoming protest: nokings.tech
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • 20 active volunteers organizing events in the Bay and Sacramento
      • Ran a Fellowship program with 10 participants upskilling in advocacy
      • Co-hosted 100+ person workshop at Mox on concentration of power, with several dozen people converting into supporters
      • Disrupted SF Board of Supervisors and the BART (media forthcoming)
      • We’ve spent 6+ months doing program design and social movement theory. We’re excited to scale exponentially in the coming weeks.
    • Funding goals: We’re actively fundraising, with a baseline goal of $2.5M in revenue for 2027. We could absorb up to $9.3M in the next year.
    • Donate: 501(c)(3)
  • Evitable: Historically focused on comms and supporting other orgs, but currently hiring an organizing director and working with Katja Grace to launch Firebell. (See comment below for full writeup!)

Outside the US

  • PauseAI UK: *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Marches, MP outreach, local events, and UK policy advocacy.
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • For the past three years has organised the biggest marches for AI safety in the world. On 21st November, held the first ever >1000-person march.
      • Organised conferences in UK and EU Parliaments.
      • See our full track record here and our donor prospectus here.
    • Donate
    • Vael: Top recommendation for UK folks; well-endorsed by UK folks I know!
  • PauseAI Global:  *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Incubates and resources national pause and x-risk advocacy chapters outside the US, such as PauseAI UK, PauseIA (France), and many more. Aims to establish that the global public wants governments to act for a pause by creating a visible, focused constituency and deep and broad community penetration and coalition work. Recently scaled up its team significantly; expect impact to increase over the coming months, especially if they invest significantly in chapter support as planned.
    • Main campaigns / accomplishments:
      • Seeded a federation of 20+ national chapters that is now consistently achieving worldwide media coverage and encounters/events with leading decision makers, making the x-risk and pause frame salient in global coverage of the AI concern movement
      • x-risk-focused content generating millions of online views despite very limited comms function
      • Conference in the EU Parliament with Stuart Russell and Brando Benifei, presenting a detailed proposal for EU leadership on AI existential safety
    • Donate. You can also ask to fund specific chapters (see list here) via PauseAI Global.
    • Vael: My top recommendation for international folks.
  • ControlAI (US, UK, Canada, Europe) *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Preventing extinction risk from ASI through an international agreement banning ASI development. Informs the public and governments, and helps them take action.
    • Main campaigns / achievements outside the US (as of Nov 2026):
      • Briefed 420+ lawmakers across the UK, Canada, and Europe on ASI extinction risk.
      • 210+ lawmakers support its UK and Canada campaign statements on AI extinction risk and action on ASI.
      • Sep 2026: its bill to ban ASI was introduced in the UK Parliament, the first bill banning ASI in any legislature. 70+ cross-party lawmakers urged the Prime Minister to back it.
      • UK grassroots supporters have sent 25k+ messages to lawmakers. 25+ lawmakers joined the UK campaign after constituents reached out.
      • Media outreach led to 130+ articles and TV segments on ASI extinction risk, incl. NYT, TIME, CNN, Fox, CBS, NewsNation, Sky News, BBC.
    • Funding info: Fundraising toward a $50M/year budget. Registered 501(c)4 in the US, Company Limited by Guarantee in the UK. If your donations are 501(c)3 restricted, get in touch, options may be available soon.
    • Donate: Contact here or email hello@controlai.org
    • Jobs
    • Vael: People especially appreciate ControlAI’s work in the UK.

 

Where you can help

Donors

Grassroots work needs much more money, through both 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4). If you’re skeptical of mass movements in general, judge the specific orgs and their track records. One may be a good fit for your views, even if not all are.

Funding is scarce here:

  • Many donors don’t consider donating outside of 501(c)(3) organizations.
  • Advisors to large donors have not historically favored grassroots work.
  • Long wait times (more than 12 months) for funding from some sources
  • Some organizations don’t take money from AI company staff, which limits their funding.

Volunteers 


US national orgs

  • Super-volunteering (volunteering 10+ hours a week) at a grassroots org: the most direct way to help. Projects are short on people who just make things happen.
  • Lobby days: trained volunteers attend meetings with lawmaker offices. More of these are needed in both DC and Sacramento.
  • Organizing or attending local events with any of these projects.
  • One-off sign-ons: March on Washington pledge to attend, MIRI statement, Do Not Accept
    • Sign-ons for specific orgs: Citizens Pledge, Stop the AI Race, ControlAI Open Statement, Humans in Control, PauseAI US petition, Pro-Human AI declaration, Freeze AI petition, etc.
  • Messages to lawmakers: options from Humans in Control, Control AI, Future of Life Institute, CallCongress.AI, etc.

US states

  • California:
    • Coordinate visits to Sacramento lawmakers by concerned citizens who live in California. (Separate from coordinating experts or AI company staff to do such visits.)
    • Vael suggests reaching out to your favorite grassroots org to see if they’re doing this already first
  • Massachusetts: Massachusetts AI Action Network
  • Texas: American Shield
  • Districts of key members of Congress: town halls and getting constituents active, especially around presidential tours.
    • People for a Pause are setting up support and training for this, and welcome volunteers. 

Outside the US

  • UK: PauseAI UK, ControlAI. Send letters to MPs.
  • Elsewhere: PauseAI Global (chapters in Netherlands, Germany, UK, Canada, France, etc.)
  • Netherlands, Singapore, Germany, and other middle powers (especially those with supply chain influence): opportunities existbut there is a need for founders and funders.


Other areas this post doesn’t cover, but that you might be interested in if this post was useful: advocacy communications projects, “grasstops” advocacy projects, political donations.

If you’re a grassroots org and want to give more detail about your work, feel free to add that in the comments! If you endorse any of these orgs, would love to also hear about that in the comments!
